summary: This document provides a framework for Data Center Network Virtualization over Layer 3 and defines a reference model with the logical components needed to design a solution.

eli5.summary: Before building a big LEGO city, you draw a plan showing which parts go where. This RFC is that plan for making virtual networks on top of a data center network.

subtitle: A shared vocabulary and reference model for building virtual tenant networks on top of an ordinary IP data center network.

tldr.problem: Large data centers host many tenants whose virtual networks must stay separate, but there was no common set of components and terms for designing overlay solutions over a Layer 3 network.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a reference model built around Network Virtualization Edges (NVEs) that tunnel tenant traffic across an IP underlay, plus the functional components and design issues any solution must address.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational framework, not a protocol, meant to guide later standards work on data center network virtualization.

facts.label: BUM methods
facts.value: Ingress replication or underlay multicast trees

today: RFC 7365 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the published NVO3 framework. It builds on the problem statement in RFC 7364.

sections.title: Purpose and Terminology
sections.content:
This framework covers Data Center (DC) Network Virtualization over Layer 3 (NVO3) tunnels. It aims to help standardize protocols and mechanisms for large-scale network virtualization. The rationale for overlays is given in RFC 7364; this document adds reference models, functional components and the technical issues to address.

It defines the vocabulary used throughout. A Tenant System is a physical or virtual system belonging to one tenant. A Virtual Network (VN) is a logical abstraction of a physical network giving L2 or L3 service to a set of Tenant Systems. The underlay is the IP network that carries tunneled packets and does not need to know it is carrying NVO3 traffic.
sections.eli5: Everyone building the virtual networks needs to use the same words. This part is the dictionary: tenants are the customers, and the underlay is the real road the virtual roads are built on.

sections.title: The DC Network and Reference Model
sections.content:
The RFC assumes a generic data center made of access switches (for example top-of-rack switches), a high-capacity intra-DC network, and DC gateways that connect to the outside world such as the Internet or VPN customers. End devices attach to access switches and may be single-homed or multihomed.

In the overlay reference model, Network Virtualization Edges (NVEs) provide a logical interconnect between Tenant Systems of the same VN. NVEs can learn reachability by exchanging information directly with each other, or by talking to an external Network Virtualization Authority (NVA). NVAs may be clustered for redundancy and scalability and appear as one logical controller.

A Tenant System can attach to an NVE locally, when both sit in the same end device, or remotely over a point-to-point connection or a switched network. For example, a VM can be a Tenant System with the NVE function in the host server, or the end device can be the Tenant System with the NVE function in the connected top-of-rack switch.
sections.eli5: Each building has a front desk (the NVE) that knows which room belongs to which customer and sends packages to the right building. Sometimes a head office (the NVA) tells the desks where everyone is.

sections.title: NVE Components and Tunneling
sections.content:
An NVE can host one or more Virtual Network Instances (VNIs). A Tenant System connects to a VNI through a Virtual Access Point (VAP), which can be a physical port or a virtual port identified by a logical interface identifier such as a VLAN ID. Each VNI defines a forwarding context holding reachability information and policies. An overlay module does the tunneling work: encapsulation and decapsulation, tenant identification and mapping.

An NVE offers one of two service types, and may offer both. An L2 NVE provides Ethernet LAN-like service, similar to VPLS or Ethernet VPN. An L3 NVE provides IP forwarding with per-tenant routing instances, similar to BGP/MPLS IP VPN (RFC 4364).

To share one underlay among many tenants, the sending NVE must encode a VN Context identifier along with the L3 tunnel information, so the destination NVE can find the right VNI. The RFC lists three approaches: one identifier per tenant (globally unique within a DC administrative domain, like IEEE VLAN IDs or I-SIDs), one per VNI (locally significant to the egress NVE, like per-VRF MPLS labels), or one per VAP.

Once the context is added, an L3 tunnel carries the frame to the egress NVE. Options include GRE, L2TP, IPsec and MPLS. Tunneling can be stateless or stateful, and stateful tunnels with configuration impose management overhead and scale constraints. When confidentiality is required, opportunistic security can serve as a stateless tunneling solution.
sections.eli5:
The front desk has a separate folder for each customer (the VNI) and a door for each customer's computers (the VAP). Some desks pass along whole rooms' worth of traffic, others only route mail by address.

Every package gets a sticker saying which customer it is for, then goes into a bigger envelope addressed to the right building. The roads only read the big envelope.

sections.title: Control Plane, Multihoming and VM Mobility
sections.content:
Control and management can be centralized, distributed, or a hybrid. NVEs must learn which VNI each Tenant System belongs to, often from a VM orchestration system, and must verify that this information is not spoofed or altered. They also keep tables binding destination VMs to egress NVE addresses, filled by the control plane, the management plane or the data plane. A control protocol carrying both MAC and IP addresses removes the need for ARP and so helps with the explosive ARP handling discussed in RFC 6820.

Multihoming raises reliability: it can be enabled from Tenant Systems into top-of-rack switches, from those into core nodes, and from core nodes into DC gateways. When an NVE gives L2 service and is not co-located with the end system, loop-avoidance techniques must be used.

VM mobility means moving a VM between servers, either stopped or suspended (cold) or running (hot). Hot mobility needs the VM's L2 and L3 addresses preserved, and NVE policies defining connectivity must be maintained.
sections.eli5: The desks need a way to learn who lives where. If a customer has two doors, mail should still get through if one door is blocked, and when a customer moves house the mail should follow.

sections.title: Issues for Overlay Designs
sections.content:
Overlays keep tunneling state at the edge, hide tenant addresses from the underlay, separate tenant address spaces from the underlay, and support a large number of virtual network identifiers. They also bring challenges: they usually cannot see underlay conditions such as utilization, coexisting overlays may not coordinate, and overlay traffic might fail to traverse firewalls and NAT devices.

  • BUM traffic: broadcast, unknown unicast and multicast can use ingress replication or underlay multicast trees, a trade-off of bandwidth against state.
  • Path MTU: the outer header can exceed the path MTU. The RFC prefers adjusting the Tenant System interface MTU or designing the underlay to accommodate the overhead, rather than relying on fragmentation.
  • NVE location: the NVE function can sit in a virtual switch, top-of-rack switch or DC gateway, judged on processing, FIB/RIB size, multicast support, fragmentation, QoS and resiliency.
  • Underlay interaction: overlays are described as selfish by nature, so resources should be provisioned and performance information may need to be exchanged with the underlay.
sections.eli5: Building virtual roads on top of real roads is handy, but the virtual roads cannot see traffic jams on the real ones, and the extra envelope makes each package bigger, so you must make sure it still fits through the door.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC looks at security from three views: the service must meet the tenant's agreed requirements, the network must be able to trust the virtual network identity on received packets, and the overlay must account for running across an underlay. VNIs and tunneling keep each tenant's data in a separate context, which gives confidentiality through separation. A tenant that needs confidentiality may encrypt its own data.

Control traffic between NVAs and NVEs must also be secured, and access to NVEs, NVAs and management systems must be limited to authorized parties. Once the tenant is verified, no integrity protection is provided on the overlay encapsulation itself (such as the VNI or destination NVE). If the underlay is not trusted to provide at least data integrity, data encryption is needed.
sections.eli5: Keeping each customer's mail in separate bins helps, but you must also lock the front desks and the head office, and check that nobody fakes a customer's name tag.
